facts.title: Named For Alfred Nobel
facts.text: Nobelium honors Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist and inventor of dynamite who endowed the Nobel Prizes. The name was proposed in 1957 by a team at the Nobel Institute for Physics in Stockholm. Even after that group's claim was disproven, the name stuck and was officially adopted, making Nobel one of the few people honored with an element.

facts.title: A Three-Lab Naming Fight
facts.text: Nobelium sits at the heart of the Cold War "Transfermium Wars" over who discovered the heaviest elements. Teams in Stockholm, Berkeley (USA), and Dubna (USSR) all claimed credit during the late 1950s and 1960s. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry eventually credited the Dubna group led by Georgy Flerov with the convincing discovery, but kept the Berkeley-backed name.

facts.title: It Does Not Exist In Nature
facts.text: Nobelium is entirely synthetic and is never found in the Earth's crust, oceans, or atmosphere. Every atom that has ever existed was made in a particle accelerator by smashing lighter nuclei together, such as firing carbon ions at a curium target. There is no natural source and no cosmic reservoir of it that we can collect.

facts.title: Gone In Less Than An Hour
facts.text: Nobelium's longest-lived isotope, nobelium-259, has a half-life of only about 58 minutes. Most other isotopes vanish in seconds or fractions of a second. This fleeting existence is why scientists have only ever produced it a handful of atoms at a time, never enough to see or weigh.

facts.title: The Rebel Plus-Two Ion
facts.text: In water, nobelium prefers the +2 oxidation state, which is highly unusual for an actinide since most of its neighbors favor +3. This stability comes from its filled 5f electron shell (a 5f14 configuration), which resists giving up an extra electron. This quirk makes nobelium chemically more like the alkaline-earth metal barium than like uranium.

facts.title: Chemistry On Single Atoms
facts.text: Because only a few atoms can be made at once, chemists study nobelium using "one-atom-at-a-time" techniques, repeating experiments thousands of times. Researchers track how lone atoms behave on ion-exchange columns to deduce properties like ionic charge. This pushes analytical chemistry to its absolute limit of sensitivity.

facts.title: First Heavy Element Laser-Probed
facts.text: In 2018, a team at the GSI laboratory in Germany measured nobelium's atomic energy levels using laser spectroscopy, a landmark for elements this heavy. It was among the first elements beyond fermium to have its atomic structure directly probed by light. The results tested how Einstein's relativity reshapes the electron orbitals of very heavy atoms.

facts.title: A Window Into Nuclear Shells
facts.text: Nobelium isotopes are prized by physicists for probing nuclear "magic numbers" and the predicted island of stability. Studying how nobelium nuclei spin and deform helps refine models of what holds super-heavy nuclei together. These experiments guide the search for even heavier, potentially longer-lived elements.

facts.title: No Job Outside The Lab
facts.text: Nobelium has no commercial, industrial, or medical uses whatsoever, and it plays no biological role in any living thing. Its extreme scarcity, rapid radioactive decay, and enormous production cost make it purely a subject of fundamental research. Its entire value lies in what it teaches us about the structure of matter.

facts.title: A Heavyweight Actinide
facts.text: With atomic number 102, nobelium is the second-to-last member of the actinide series, just before lawrencium. It is one of the transuranium elements, meaning it sits beyond uranium on the periodic table. Element 102 marks the near-completion of the 5f electron shell that defines the entire actinide family.
